Story idea (the user's own words):
<user_input>It is autumn in Baden, and the chestnut trees along the path to the old Stadtturm are shedding leaves the colour of copper. Ethan is nine and Lily is six, and their family has moved into a flat in the Altstadt only a week ago — their parents James and Rachel still surrounded by boxes, their grandmother Margaret visiting to help and fussing cheerfully over everything. Every afternoon, the children from the neighbourhood gather in the square near the old tower, and Ethan and Lily can see them from the window. Ethan wants a friend before school begins on Monday; so does Lily, with rather more noise about it. But every time the two of them go down to join the group, something goes wrong — a word lands badly, a turn is skipped, a moment tips — and they find themselves walking home again with no one beside them. Monday is coming, and a whole school full of faces none of them know.</user_input>

# ARC

1. One week after the move, the boxes still stood shut in the Altstadt flat in Baden: James labelled them in the wrong order, Rachel boiled water for tea, and Margaret pinned a red woollen hat on Lily and said, "Hold still, chick, hold still — a count is a thing you sit right through, no wriggling."
2. From the window Ethan and Lily watched the neighbourhood children playing hide-and-seek in the square below the old tower; Ethan said they had to find one friend before Monday, because on Monday they would walk into the school by the tower where every one of those children already knew each other, but Lily shouted, "Two! One each! I am going down now."
3. In the square the children repeated their rule before every round — nobody answers when their name is called, because answering puts you out — and Ethan and Lily watched one boy stay silent behind a bin until the counting stopped; but Lily could not wait through the count, therefore she burst out of her hiding place early and gave away the smallest girl, the one in the red duffel coat.
4. The boy in the striped scarf, who did the counting and kept the rules, said the round was spoiled and that they were not playing; Ethan and Lily climbed the stairs alone, Lily cried on the landing, and Rachel sat beside her but did not go down and speak to the children for them.
5. On Saturday Ethan tried again, but he was turning a chestnut over in his fingers while the rule was repeated, therefore when the boy called his name as a test he answered out loud and spoiled a second round; embarrassed, Ethan said it was a baby's game and that his old street played it properly, so the boy in the striped scarf said, "The rule is, you don't come back," and now they were disliked instead of merely unknown, which was worse.
6. At dusk Lily walked along the chestnut path to the covered wooden bridge, squeezed into the gap behind the log pile stacked at the bridge mouth, and decided it was the best hiding place in Baden; Ethan found her there and pulled her out by the arm, therefore the top log slid down across the mouth of the gap and the red hat slipped off deeper inside — neither of them saw it, but the girl in the red duffel coat saw it from the chestnut path.
7. At supper Margaret asked after the hat and Lily could not say where it had gone, which made Lily ashamed; Ethan felt flat, because Sunday was the last day and both their tries were used up.
8. On Sunday evening Lily stood at the window, and when the tower clock struck six and the children ran home up the lane, she noticed that the red duffel coat was not among them.
9. Ethan and Lily ran down and told the boy in the striped scarf, who counted the coats going up the lane and found himself one short; but he said her big sister always took her home, that they were inventing it to be let back in, and he did not move.
10. Therefore Ethan said the true thing out loud: he had answered his name because he had not been listening, and he had called their game babyish because he was frightened that nobody would pick him — the boy in the striped scarf looked at his shoes, said, "The rule is, you look before you go home," and came.
11. They called her name through the lanes and no answer came back, therefore Lily said she knew one place that was out of bounds and led them down the chestnut path to the covered bridge, because the gap behind the logs was hers and she had shown it to nobody.
12. Behind the log pile the smallest girl was wedged past the fallen log, holding the red hat she had crawled in to fetch back for Lily; she whispered that she had heard them calling but had been too frightened to make any sound, and she was too frightened to be pulled.
13. Lily crawled in, said she was sorry for giving her away on Friday, held her hand and sat still beside her through a whole slow count — the same Lily who could not sit through twenty — while Ethan ran back for the others and the boy in the striped scarf lifted the top logs away one by one until the girl could come out.
14. They walked back to the tower with the smallest one holding Lily's hand and the hat back on Lily's head, where James and Rachel stood waiting beside the girl's big sister, who had believed all evening that she had gone up the lane with the rest; the boy in the striped scarf admitted he had been about to go home, told Lily she counted far too fast, and asked her to do the counting on Tuesday anyway — and on Monday morning Ethan and Lily walked to the school by the tower inside a group of children who knew their names, Lily saying she was not frightened any more, only impatient, impatient for four o'clock.

Challenges taken:
